## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahiṁsarājajātaka* (Ja 278), translated as *The Buffalo King*, is a narrative belonging to the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the narrative framework recorded in the tradition, the Buddha recounted this past life while residing at Jetavana with reference to an impertinent monkey [SuttaCentral]. In the story, the Bodhisatta is born as a buffalo who is repeatedly tormented and defecated upon by a disrespectful monkey [Appleton 2010]. Instead of retaliating, the buffalo chooses to patiently endure the mistreatment, reflecting that the monkey, emboldened by this leniency, will eventually behave the same way toward another animal and meet its demise, thereby sparing the Bodhisatta both the harassment and the moral fault of taking life [Appleton 2010].

The narrative corresponds in theme to the *Mahiṁsarājacariya* (Cp 15) in the *Cariyāpiṭaka*, where the story exemplifies the Bodhisatta’s perfection of forbearance [SuttaCentral]. Automated text-reuse analysis via DharmaNexus indicates that the canonical verses share three passages with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), with the most extensive match covering segments §1.1–2.4 [DharmaNexus]. No cross-language alignments meet the reporting threshold in DharmaNexus [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral catalogs four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
